blocks.text: Since Richard Sutton’s influential essay in 2019, the concept of the bitter lesson has guided much of modern progress in AI. This concept espouses general methods that leverage computation and learn with scale, as free of human-engineered priors as possible. Our interpretation is that, fundamentally, intelligence is about learning from raw data: autonomously finding patterns, building abstractions, and developing meaning from messy low-level inputs, ideally end-to-end and as data-efficiently as possible. As AI advances into complex domains such as science, robotics, and biology – where data is scarce and often difficult for humans to understand, let alone engineer for – internalizing this philosophy to develop more general learning algorithms is more important than ever.

blocks.text: Language models are perhaps AI’s biggest success story today, and largely embrace the bitter lesson. Their abilities are largely attributable to scaling a few simple algorithms such as the Transformer architecture, next-token prediction, reinforcement learning, and test-time computation. However, they still rely on hand-crafted encoding steps such as tokenizers, which severely hinder their ability to learn end-to-end from the underlying data. Towards unlocking another step change of scaling, we believe that developing byte-level language models is foundational for AI progress – not just for improving standalone LLMs, but also as a litmus test for general learning methods. If we can’t even learn language well from characters and bytes, what right do we have to make progress on the next frontier?

blocks.text: Hierarchical networks (H-Nets) compress data through a recursive, data-dependent dynamic chunking process.

inlines.text: Hierarchical networks (H-Nets) compress data through a recursive, data-dependent dynamic chunking process.

blocks.text: The terminology was inspired by the existing concept of chunking in cognitive psychology, which is an essential part of human intelligence. We believe it is also necessary for the frontier of artificial intelligence.

blocks.text: In the context of language modeling, the idea is to build new learning primitives that allow models to recursively chunk low-level data into higher-level meaning: characters into words, words into phrases, phrases into concepts.

inlines.text: In the context of language modeling, the idea is to build new learning primitives that allow models to recursively chunk low-level data into higher-level meaning: characters into words, words into phrases, phrases into concepts.

blocks.text: In the context of this post, for the most part, one can think of hierarchical networks as replacing tokenization. Instead of pre-processing data from bytes into tokens (fixed chunks of bytes), H-Nets perform the chunking dynamically directly inside the model. Furthermore, the signature characterization of H-Nets is that they hierarchically perform this chunking end-to-end. In contrast, standard tokenized language models and even other alternatives (some of which we’ll see in Post II) employ multiple stages of training, and the process of chunking / tokenizing the data is performed entirely offline.

blocks.text: Details: Tokenization and BPELanguage models don’t read text directly but instead take as input a sequence of tokens from a fixed vocabulary. A natural vocabulary is the 256 byte values, producing one token per UTF-8 byte. Byte-level sequences, however, are long and expensive for standard language models to process. Tokenization aims to alleviate this problem by compressing the byte sequence into frequently occurring chunks. The most common approach, Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), starts from the 256 bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent pair of adjacent tokens on a fixed training corpus, until the vocabulary reaches a set size (e.g. 128k for Llama-3). On our data mix, each BPE token covers about 4.57 bytes, making sequences much shorter than at the byte level. However, this compression is fixed, and tokenization remains one of the last parts of the language-modeling pipeline that is designed by hand rather than learned.

blocks.text: H-Net architectureTwo-stage byte H-NetDecoderDechunkingDecoderDechunkingMain networkChunkingEncoderChunkingEncoderFigure 1. The hierarchical network (H-Net) architecture. Inputs go through a series of 5 modules: (1) an encoder reads the inputs, such as bytes; (2) a learned chunking step compresses them into a few chunks; (3) the main network operates over coarse chunks (analogous to tokens); (4) the chunks are decompressed back into the input resolution and summed with a residual; (5) a decoder finishes processing the combined representations. A 1-stage H-Net performs one level of dynamic chunking; the main network itself can be an H-Net, allowing the chunking process to be recursively nested. Hover over different bytes to see how they’re routed through this 2-stage hierarchical network!

blocks.text: As with many architecture papers, the original paper on hierarchical networks focused on tuning language models of particular fixed sizes and data horizons (e.g. ~1.3B-parameter models on 100B tokens from FineWeb-Edu have been very common). Although they looked very promising, a missing piece was the lack of compute-optimal scaling laws, now a standard way to measure pretraining innovations. For example, Kimi’s popular innovations on Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and attention residuals measured compute multipliers of 1.16x and 1.25x, respectively.

We then converted each rung to a byte-level H-Net as a drop-in replacement, reusing the BPE backbone architecture and hyperparameters.

blocks.text: In-corpus BPE tokenizer: LLMs generally use off-the-shelf BPE tokenizers; an advantage of H-Nets is that they learn their chunking directly on the training distribution. To be extra careful, we also trained a BPE tokenizer on the corpus. We used this for the BPE scaling laws below, which ended up resulting in about a 1.1x compute gain on both validation loss and downstream evals (so the H-Net would have an even greater compute multiplier against a standard off-the-shelf tokenizer!).

blocks.text: The BPE tokenizer’s vocab size is 128k, matching the Llama-3 tokenizer that we were working off of. The in-corpus tokenizer compressed the dataset slightly more, increasing the average BPE token length from 4.45 (Llama-3 tokenizer) to 4.57. Measured in tokens of the in-corpus BPE tokenizer, the training dataset comprised 64.7% English, 23.7% code, 6.1% math, and 5.5% multilingual.

blocks.text: Creating a robust BPE baseline

For our baseline, we fit a well-tuned scaling law for a standard BPE Transformer. To do this, we constructed a scaling ladder, following modern scaling recipes such as Kimi and MAI, fully defining a family of models by the number of layers L. We set the hidden dimension D to a multiple of 128 such that the aspect ratio D/L is approximately 75. For all models, we use multi-head attention with the number of heads equal to the number of layers and a fixed head dimension of 128. For the MLPs, we use SwiGLU layers with the intermediate dimension set to 3.6D, again rounding to the nearest multiple of 128.1

blocks.text: An equivalent H-Net ladder

Because H-Nets over bytes are so different from standard tokenized models, it’s highly nontrivial to compare them directly. There are so many moving parts: how many stages of chunking, the respective compression rates, the architecture configurations of each stage (outer vs. inner networks), and the hyperparameters for each component.

blocks.text: Evaluations: We examined standard downstream evaluation suites such as Paloma and OLMES, each of which consists of a mixture of dozens of datasets and tasks spanning human languages and domains (code, math, etc.). For each one, we measured the “soft accuracy” of a model as the bits-per-byte it assigns to the correct answer. Re-fitting compute-to-bpb scaling laws to each suite, we see that the gap between H-Nets and BPE Transformers grows further to around 2x.

blocks.text: Intuitively, we hypothesize these phenomena arise for a few reasons:

inlines.text: Intuitively, we hypothesize these phenomena arise for a few reasons:

H-Nets perform better on new distributions in general because they learn how to create semantic concepts from lower-level data, which generalize better. This is reflected in the rise from in-distribution (1.28x) to downstream evaluations (2.06x), and from in-domain programming languages (median 2.04x) to out-of-domain programming languages (median 3.10x).
will discuss out-of-distribution transfer in much more detail.

H-Nets are better on data that’s difficult to tokenize, in the sense of lacking a small vocabulary of reusable patterns. This is particularly evident in code, which is very dynamic and possesses a wide range of whitespace and symbols, syntax structure, and variable names (essentially an infinite vocabulary even over Latin characters!). Pre-defined tokens are less likely to capture the full range of semantics.

, we show that H-Nets learn semantics on the fly at inference time, for example being able to learn variable names in code as one token; we hypothesize this is one particular mechanism that lets them excel at code.

They can involve multiple stages of chunking, compared to a single static phase by BPE.

blocks.text: Architecture: We built a two-stage hierarchical network over bytes.

inlines.text: : We built a two-stage hierarchical network over bytes.
The outermost (byte-level) stage uses four Mamba-2 layers in the encoder and four in the decoder.
The next stage adds a sliding-window attention block and four more Mamba-2 layers on each side.
The main network is a 40-layer Transformer with the same per-layer shape as SmolLM3, with global attention in every layer.
The compression ratios were set according to prior work (targeting 4x and 2x in the two outer encoder stages).

blocks.text: Where are the FLOPs spent?

Unlike the scaling ladders, we focused more on aligning with the philosophy of hierarchical networks: allowing the model to perform dynamic chunking in multiple stages, ideally following the semantics of the data. This made matching all axes to the baseline impossible, as parameters and compute get spent in very different ways. We aimed to control for FLOPs/byte, so that every minibatch of training sees the same underlying data and spends the same amount of compute as the baseline.

inlines.text: Unlike the scaling ladders, we focused more on aligning with the philosophy of hierarchical networks: allowing the model to perform dynamic chunking in multiple stages, ideally following the semantics of the data. This made matching all axes to the baseline impossible, as parameters and compute get spent in very different ways. We aimed to control for
, so that every minibatch of training sees the same underlying data and spends the same amount of compute as the baseline.

The compression ratios were set so the main network sees roughly one position for every 8 bytes (the trained model ends up at ~7.6×). Compared to ~4.5 bytes per Llama-3 token, this is about 40% fewer tokens than SmolLM3 processes on the same text.
That saving trades off for the outer encoder/decoder stages, which account for about 43% of the H-Net’s FLOPs (compared to 8% for the embedding and LM head in the tokenized Transformer).
The resulting models are compute matched to within 2% FLOPs/byte.

blocks.text: Discussion: Data controlsDespite our effort to control for data and compute fairly, in hindsight we realized it’s still not obvious what a proper methodology should be. For example, let’s look at English vs. code: the reason SmolLM3’s token mix of 73.2% / 12.0% respectively becomes 76.5% / 10.3% at the byte level is because tokenizers compress English more (see Figure 8b), which itself is an artifact of BPE tokenization (it spends more effort compressing more frequently appearing data, so it’s tied to the arbitrary data distribution).On the other hand, the philosophy of H-Nets is to compress data according to an “intrinsic” notion of compressibility and semantics. For example, we find that H-Nets compress code a lot more because code is naturally compressible; and we attribute much of H-Net’s improvements on code to this ability to understand the data better. But at the same time, this means that H-Nets spend less compute on code (because the same piece of code data gets turned into far fewer chunks sent into the main network) relative to the BPE baseline! So would a better way to control it be to let the models spend similar amounts of compute per source instead?In short, BPE models and H-Nets can compress subdomains in opposite ways - for example, BPE compresses code less than English while H-Nets compress it more - so it’s impossible to both data- and compute- match, and the right way to compare models is subtle. blocks.text: New emergent behaviors: in-context tokenization
In-context tokenization

An H-Net’s tokenization not only changes over training time, but can also evolve during inference, which we call in-context tokenization. We previously discussed some simple cases of how boundaries of H-Nets are context-based, and not pattern-based. In Figure 11, we highlight four interesting examples of the in-context tokenization:

blocks.text: One such area is audio, a core focus of Cartesia, where the inability of models to autonomously abstract raw audio into phonemes and words represents a major bottleneck toward multimodal speech-to-speech models (and in fact was a motivation for us to start investigating H-Nets years ago!).

blocks.text: More broadly, bytes are not necessarily a universal encoding for all domains. Most domains have a concept of “primitive building blocks”, such as characters or bytes for language, pixels for images and video, waveforms for audio, nucleotides for biology, and so on. We’ve started thinking of different modalities as being built from various base atoms, and of so-called atomic models as the truly bitter-lesson-pilled way to build powerful foundation models for multimodality. We highlight some examples of additional domains.

blocks.text: Biology (DNA)

DNA is the lowest-level programming language of biology. Depending on the context, its natural level of abstraction, and therefore its natural primitive units, changes drastically. Because of this, we hypothesized that H-Net’s dynamic tokenization would be significantly more effective than a static tokenization scheme on the DNA domain.

blocks.text: H-Net was trained only on the next-letter prediction task for prokaryote (bacterial and archaeal) genomes, so the adherence of H-Net’s token segmentation to biology’s natural structure in the human genome is purely emergent behavior. Here we display some of these examples:

inlines.text: H-Net was trained only on the next-letter prediction task for prokaryote (bacterial and archaeal) genomes, so the adherence of H-Net’s token segmentation to biology’s natural structure in the human genome is purely emergent behavior. Here we display some of these examples:

blocks.text: Example1 of 5H-Net chunksHuman chromosome 6, histone gene H2BC17 · never seen in trainingone chunk per band1st letter of a codon2nd letter of a codon3rd letter of a codonstart / stop codonpromoterhairpinend of the RNA86 chunks in 680 letters · 7.9 letters eachFigure 14a. A whole human histone gene (H2BC17): coding and non-coding regions. Histones are the proteins that DNA wraps around. This example window runs from the gene's promoter (non-coding region), through its 126 codons (coding), and to the hairpin at which the RNA terminates (non-coding region). Within the coding region, the unit is the codon. H-Net learns chunks that start on codon borders and almost all run one to three codons long . The non-coding DNA on either side (the promoter region before and the termination signal after) has far less structure and is not read in threes. There the H-Net draws chunks that are long and less structured .

blocks.text: Quick primer on Biology/DNADNA and genes. DNA is a string of four letters: A, C, G, and T. A gene is the stretch of DNA responsible for producing an RNA sequence, which is usually translated into a protein. Only its coding region actually spells out the protein, while the DNA around it is far less constrained and more information-sparse: the promoter region before it, the signal that ends the RNA after it. They control when and how the protein is made, not what it is. Additionally, in human genes, introns, non-coding regions that sit in the middle of the coding region, are spliced out and also do not contribute to the protein sequence.Codons and the reading frame. The coding region is read three letters at a time, from a start codon (usually ATG) to a stop codon (TAA, TAG, or TGA). Each three-letter codon names one amino acid in a protein sequence. Where reading starts sets the reading frame: shift it by one letter and every codon downstream changes.

blocks.text: Some notable learned behaviors:

inlines.text: Inside a gene, the H-Net router settles on a different atomic unit depending on what it is reading; we see biologically aligned treatments of:
Robustness: H-Net’s learned codon grid isn’t fixed; where two coding regions overlap and the second is offset, H-Net’s boundaries adapt quickly
In a transfer RNA (tRNA) gene, the natural unit shrinks to a single letter. H-Net boundaries learn to adhere to this new natural unit
Large sections of repeats in DNA are typically information-sparse, so in a repeat, the natural biological unit grows to the whole repeat

blocks.text: Interestingly, as one may expect, a lot of these biologically adherent behaviors aren’t learned until late into training, as shown through the learning trajectory animation. The late onset of these behaviors highlights the nontriviality of the “tokenization task” in the DNA domain, and supports the thesis that hand-crafted tokenization schemes would be even more difficult and less effective in multimodal domains than in language.

blocks.text: Vision

Hierarchical networks are naturally defined for one-dimensional sequential data, where chunking and segmentation are intuitive. Extending them to higher-dimensional modalities, however, presents a significant technical challenge – and simultaneously a great opportunity, as vision is a domain naturally suited to hierarchies. In ongoing research, we’ve developed new techniques to apply H-Nets to N-dimensional data such as images and videos. When integrated into a pixel-space diffusion model, H-Nets not only improve generation quality, but also uncover unsupervised semantic concepts directly from raw data – mirroring the emergent behaviors we saw with language.

blocks.text: In more detail, we take a standard pixel-space flow-matching baseline JiT, and replace its backbone with a multi-dimensional H-Net. Just as with 1D H-Nets, the model learns both where to chunk and how much to compress. This allows it to dynamically reallocate compute across three axes: spatially (focusing on detailed regions over simple ones), integration time (varying effort by denoising step), and samples (allocating more compute on complex images). Consequently, the model consolidates homogeneous or low-information areas and focuses on salient details, and discovers semantic segmentations of the image completely without supervision. A final interesting detail is that unlike existing token-merging methods that rely on the similarity of contiguous patches, our 2D H-Net doesn’t enforce local grouping. Because of this, the model often appears to infer underlying 3D structure from flat 2D projections. For instance, it routinely groups disjointed background regions into a single coherent chunk, even when they are separated in the image by occluding foreground objects.
